newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria president sees no currency board backlash.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria president sees no currency board backlash.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov said on Monday he did not predict any adverse reaction to introduction of a fixed exchange rate regime pegging the lev to the German mark from Tuesday.
"The currency board is not a remedy for all problems but neither is it a poison that will destroy Bulgaria," Stoyanov told reporters after signing the new banking law.
Used properly it could be a remedy for many of Bulgaria's economic problems, he said, a view echoed by Prime Minister Ivan Kostov, who forecast a slowing of inflation in August.
"I am optimistic that inflation will be lower in August than ever before," he told reporters.
The currency board system bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks, and requires that levs in circulation be fully covered by foreign exchange reserves.
The central bank guarantees that it will have one mark for every thousand levs in circulation, freezing the exchange rate at that level.
Bulgaria's economy has been subject to many of the system's restrictions for the past couple of months. Inflation has slowed and exchange rates have stabilised in anticipation of the peg.

Martin Zaimov, head of the Issue Department at the Bulgarian National Bank, said the bank would start the currency board on Tuesday with 2.7 billion mark ($1.6 billion) gross foreign exchange reserves to cover liabilities of 2.2 trillion levs ($1.3 billion).

"We have sufficient cover for our lev liabilities," Zaimov, also a BNB deputy governor, told Reuters Financial Television. "The aggregate amount is 2.7 billion German marks and that consists of gold, foreign currency and foreign securities."
On the interbank market, the lev closed around 994-995 per mark, slightly firmer than the opening 994-996 due to high foreign currency supply.
Exchange bureaux were buying marks at 980-985 levs and selling at 994-998 levs on Monday, and buying dollars at 1,685-1,695 levs and selling at 1,710-1,720 levs.

Dealer Katya Ilieva said business had been brisk in the past few days and she expected it to continue under the new system. "We expect to deal mainly with dollars and other currencies as the BNB will trade only with marks," she said.
Under the currency board the central bank will buy marks at 995 levs and sell at 1,000 levs.

Dealer Michail Uzunov said his bureau would calculate commission on lev/mark trade according to the central bank's spread between buy and sell rates. The margin on trade in other currencies would depend on the international markets and on the domestic interbank foreign exchange market.
The currency board mechanism is being introduced for an indefinite period, and economists say its restrictions will help to bring Bulgaria closer to other European economies.
Currency boards have been used to repair crumbling financial systems and curb inflation in countries such as Argentina, Lithuania and Estonia. The system has also been proposed for Bosnia.
Imposition of a currency board stops governments from printing money which is not backed by reserves, and prevents the central bank from directly funding the budget deficit.
The International Monetary Fund proposed the mechanism for Bulgaria after the previous programme was suspended because the former Socialist government failed to meet its targets.

Bulgaria's economy ground to a halt last year after a run on the lev caused by the fragility of the banking sector and foreign exchange market. Interest rate increases failed to restore confidence, and once foreign exchange reserves were exhausted, the lev crashed. -- Sofia Newsroom +359-2 91188 ($ = 1.739 German Marks) ($ = 1728 Bulgarian Levs)
